source_text: Oportuerat etiam sepultorem domini prophetari ac iam tunc merito benedici, si nec mulierum illarum officium praeterit prophetia, quae ante lucem conuenerunt ad sepulcrum cum odorum paratura. de hoc enim per Osee: et quaerent, inquit, faciem meam; ante lucem uigilabunt ad me dicentes: eamus et conuertamur ad dominum, quia ipse eripuit [dixit] et curabit nos, percussit et miserebitur nostri, sanabit nos post biduum, in die tertia resurgemus. quis enim haec non credat in recogitatu mulierum illarum uolutata inter dolorem praesentis destitutionis, qua percussae sibi uidebantur a domino, et spem resurrectionis ipsius, qua restitutuiri se arbitrabantur? corpore autem non inuento sublata erat sepultura eius de medio secundum Esaiam. sed et duo ibidem angeli apparuerunt. tot fere laterensibus uti solebat in duobus testibus consistens dei sermo. reuertentes quoque a sepulcro mulieres et ab illa angelorum uisione prospiciebatEsaias: mulieres, inquit, [uenite] uenientes a uisione, uenite, ad renuntiandam scilicet domini resurrectionem. Bene autem,I quod incredulitas discipulorum perseuerabat, ut in finem usque defensio nostra consisteret Christum legum non alium se discipulis edidisse quam prophetarum. nam cum duo ex illis iter agerent et dominus eis adhaesisset, non comparens quod ipse esset, etiam dissimulans de conscientia rei gestae: nos autem putabamus, inquiunt, ipsum esse redemptorem Israhelis, utique suum Christum, id est creatoris. adeo nec alium se ediderat illis. ceterum non existimarent eum creatoris,I et cum creatoris existimaretur, non sustinuisset hanc de se existimationem, si non is esset, qui existimabatur. aut ipse! erit auctor erroris et praeuaricator ueritatis aduersus dei optimi titulum. sed nec post resurrectionem alium se eis ostendit quam quem existimatum sibi dixerant. plane inuectus est in illos: o insensati et tardi corde in non credendo omnibus, \'quae locutus est ad uos.\' quaenam locutus? alterius se dei esse? proba, et manus dedo. an eadem et angeli ad mulieres: rememoramini, quae locutus sit uobis in Galilaea dicens, quod oportet tradi filium hominis et crucifigi et tertia die resurgere? et quare oportebat, nisi quia ita a deo creatore scriptum? igitur increpuit illos ut de sola passione scandalizatos et ut dubios de fide resurrectionis adnuntiatae sibi a feminis, per quae non crediderant ipsum fuisse, quem existimauerant. itaque quod existimauerant, id uolens credi se eum se confirmabat, quem existimauerant, creatoris scilicet Christum, redemptorem Israhelis. De corporis autem ueritate quid potest clarius? cum haesitantibus eis, ne phantasma esset, immo phantasma credentibus: quid turbati estis? (in quit,) et quid cogitationes subeunt in corda uestra? uidete manus meas et pedes, quia ipse ego sum, quoniam spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me habentem uidetis. et Marcion quaedam contraria sibi illa, credo, industria eradere de euangelio suo noluit, ut ex his, quae eradere potuit nec erasit, illa, quae erasit, aut negetur erasisse aut merito erasisse dicatur; nec parcit nisi eis, quae non minus aliter interpretando quam delendo subuertit. uult itaque sic dictum: spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me uidetis habentem, quasi ad spiritum referatur sicut me uidetis habentem, id est non habentem ossa, sicut et spiritus. et quae ratio tortuositatis istius, cum simpliciter pronuntiare potuisset:. \'quia spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me uidetis non habentem\'? cur autem inspectui eorum manus et pedes suos offert, quae membra ex ossibus constant, si ossa non habebat? cur adicit: et scitote, quia ego sum, quem scilicet corporeum retro nouerant? aut si phantasma erat usquequaque, cur illos phantasma credentes increpabat? atquin adhuc eis non credentibus propterea cibum desiderauit, ut se ostenderet etiam dentes habere. Impleuimus, ut opinor, sponsionem. exhibuimus legum Christum prophetarum doctrinis sententiis adfectibus sensibus uirtutibus passionibus etiam resun-ectione non alium quam creatoris, siquidem et apostolos mittens ad praedicandum uniuersis nationibus in omnem terram exire sonum eorum et in terminos terrae uoces eorum psalmum adimplendo praecepit. misereor tui, Marcion; frustra laborasti. Christus enim Iesus in euangelio tuo meus est.
thought_title: Christ Confirmed by Prophecies and Resurrection
pass_a_gloss: It was also fitting for the Lord's burial to be prophesied and for it to be deservedly blessed even then, if prophecy did not pass over the service of those women who had gathered at the tomb before dawn with preparations for fragrances. For concerning this, through Hosea, it says: 'They will seek my face; they will be vigilant for me before dawn, saying: Let us go and turn to the Lord, because he has torn and will heal us, he has struck and will have mercy on us, he will heal us after two days, on the third day we will rise.' Who would not believe that these things were thought by those women, who were rolling them around in their minds amidst the pain of the present destitution, by which they seemed to themselves to have been struck by the Lord, and the hope of his resurrection, by which they thought they would be restored? However, the burial of his body was removed from the midst, according to Isaiah, because it was not found. But also, two angels appeared there, almost always using two witnesses, as is the custom of God's word. Also, Isaiah foresaw the women returning from the tomb and from that vision of the angels, saying: 'Come, women, coming from the vision, come to announce the Lord's resurrection.' It is good, indeed, that the disciples' unbelief persisted, so that our defense might consist until the end that Christ taught his disciples the laws, not another, but the prophets. For when two of them were on a journey and the Lord had joined them, not appearing as he was, but also disguising the knowledge of the thing done, they said: 'We thought he was the redeemer of Israel, certainly his Christ, that is, the creator's.' So, he had not presented another to them. Moreover, they did not think him to be the creator's, and when he was thought to be the creator's, he would not have endured this opinion about himself if he were not the one who was thought. Or would he be the author of error and the transgressor of truth against the title of the good God? But not even after the resurrection did he show himself to them as another than the one they had thought. Clearly, he was reproaching them: 'O foolish and slow-hearted ones, not believing all that he spoke to you.' What did he speak? That he was of another God? Prove it, and give me your hand. Or did the angels say the same to the women: 'Remember what he said to you in Galilee, saying that it was necessary for the Son of Man to be betrayed and crucified and to rise on the third day?' And why was it necessary, if not because it was thus written by the creator God? Therefore, he rebuked them because they were scandalized by the passion alone and because they were doubting the faith of the resurrection announced to them by the women, through which they did not believe him to be the one they thought. Thus, what they thought, he, wanting to be believed, confirmed that he was the one they thought, namely, the creator's Christ, the redeemer of Israel. What can be clearer about the truth of the body? When they were hesitating, lest it be a phantom, indeed, believing it to be a phantom: 'Why are you troubled?' he said, 'and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and feet, because I myself am, since a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having.' And Marcion, I believe, did not want to erase certain things contrary to himself from his gospel, so that from those things which he could have erased but did not, those things which he erased might either be denied or be said to have been erased deservedly. Nor does he spare except those things which, by interpreting them otherwise rather than deleting them, he subverts. He wants it to be said thus: 'A spirit does not have bones, as you see me having,' as if it were referred to the spirit, as you see me having, that is, not having bones, just like a spirit. And what is the reason for this twisting, when he could have spoken simply: 'Because a spirit does not have bones, as you see me not having'? Why, then, does he offer his hands and feet for their inspection, which members consist of bones, if he did not have bones? Why does he add: 'And know that I am,' whom they certainly knew to be bodily before? Or, if it was a phantom, why did he rebuke them, believing it to be a phantom? But, indeed, he still desired food from them, not believing, so that he might show himself to have teeth as well. We have fulfilled, I think, the promise. We have shown the Christ of the laws, the prophets' doctrines, sentences, affections, senses, virtues, passions, and even resurrection, not another than the creator's, since he also sent the apostles to preach to all nations, to go out into all the earth, and to fill the psalm, saying: 'Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.' I pity you, Marcion; you have labored in vain. For Christ Jesus in your gospel is mine.

pass_b_english: The Lord's burial had to be prophesied, and it deserved to be blessed even then, since prophecy did not overlook the service of those women who gathered at the tomb before dawn with spices. For through Hosea Scripture says: "They will seek my face; they will be vigilant for me before dawn, saying: 'Let us go and turn to the Lord, because he has torn and will heal us, he has struck and will have mercy on us, he will heal us after two days, on the third day we will rise'" (Hosea 5:15–6:2). Who would not believe that these things were turning in those women's minds amid the pain of their present destitution, by which they seemed struck by the Lord, and amid the hope of his resurrection, by which they thought they would be restored? However, because his body was not found, his burial was removed from the midst, according to Isaiah (Isaiah 53:9). Also, two angels appeared there, since God's word customarily establishes its case on two witnesses. Isaiah also foresaw the women returning from the tomb and from that vision of the angels: "Come, women coming from the vision, come to announce the Lord's resurrection" (Isaiah 52:7). It is a good thing that the disciples' unbelief persisted, so that our defense might stand to the end: Christ taught his disciples the Law, not some other, but the prophets. When two of them were traveling and the Lord joined them, he did not appear as he truly was, even disguising his knowledge of what had happened. They said: "We thought he was the redeemer of Israel, certainly his Christ, that is, the Creator's" (Luke 24:21). So he had not presented any other to them. Yet they did not think he was the Creator's, and when he was thought to be the Creator's, he would not have tolerated this opinion about himself if he were not the one they thought he was. Or would he be the author of error and the falsifier of truth against the title of the good God? But not even after the resurrection did he show himself to them as anyone other than the one they had believed. Clearly he reproached them: "O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken" (Luke 24:25). What did he speak? That he was the God of another? Prove it, and I will give you my hand. Or did the angels say the same to the women: "Remember what he told you in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered and crucified and rise on the third day?" (Luke 24:6–7). And why was it necessary, if not because it was thus written by the Creator God? Therefore he rebuked them because they were scandalized by the passion alone and doubted the resurrection faith announced to them by the women, through which they did not believe him to be the one they had thought. Thus, what they thought, he—wanting that to be believed—confirmed that he was the one they thought: the Creator's Christ, the Redeemer of Israel. What can be clearer about the truth of the body? When they were hesitating, lest it be a phantom—indeed, believing it to be a phantom—he said: "Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have" (Luke 24:38–39). Marcion, I believe, did not want to erase certain things contrary to himself from his gospel, so that from those things he could have erased but did not, the things he did erase might either be denied or said to have been erased deservedly. Nor does he spare except those things which, by interpreting them otherwise rather than deleting them, he subverts. He wants it to read: "A spirit does not have bones, as you see me having," as if it referred to the spirit—"as you see me having"—that is, not having bones, just like a spirit. What is the reason for this twisting, when he could have spoken simply: "Because a spirit does not have bones, as you see me not having"? Why then does he offer his hands and feet for their inspection, which members consist of bones, if he did not have bones? Why does he add: "And know that I am," whom they certainly knew to be bodily before? Or if it was a phantom throughout, why did he rebuke them for believing it to be a phantom? Indeed, while they still did not believe, he asked for food so that he might show he also has teeth. We have fulfilled, I think, the pledge. We have shown the Christ of the Law—by the prophets' doctrines, sentences, affections, senses, virtues, passions, and even resurrection—to be none other than the Creator's, since he also sent the apostles to preach to all nations, to go out into all the earth, and to fulfill the psalm: "Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world" (Psalm 19:4). I pity you, Marcion; you have labored in vain. For Christ Jesus in your gospel is mine.
